title: Cars to be banned from Cheesman Park (for now)
summary: Buses, cyclists and pedestrians are still welcome.
content: Cars are a rare breed in Cheesman Park, with personal automobiles only permitted on one street through the popular green space. Now, a city project on 12th Avenue could render them extinct — at least temporarily. The city is piloting changes to 12th Avenue that will create a “neighborhood zone,” allowing pedestrians and cyclists to feel more comfortable. The change is part of the city’s “Safer Streets Neighborhood Zones” program, which will test temporary changes at four locations across Denver. The city will install signs and markings that discourage drivers from using 12th Avenue in the blocks west and east of the park. As drivers reach Cheesman Park, signs will warn personal automobiles not to enter. The 10 Route bus, which has a stop in Cheesman Park, will still be allowed in the park. The changes will be installed soon, with the pilot continuing into the spring. The city will also install pilot projects to restrict traffic near Dora Moore Elementary, reduce speeds on 14th Avenue in the West Colfax neighborhood, and reroute traffic near Baker’s Dailey Park. Many of Denver’s major parks were completely closed off to cars during COVID-19 era shutdowns to make room for people to gather outside. But as the world started to come back from quarantine, the city opted to keep many parks car-light, not completely car-free. The city is also asking residents to share their experiences traversing the neighborhood about its four pilot programs. Once the pilot period is over, the city will decide whether to keep, modify or remove the temporary treatments. The project also could lead to long-term changes.

title: Gandalf the White (and all the other felines we met at Denver Cat Fest)
summary: "He has a quiet confidence about him, almost as though he knows he’s something special."
content: Gandalf the White graced a stage at the National Western Center earlier this month. But this wizard hailed from Glenwood Springs, not Middle-earth, and he was not a tall old man. He was a cat — a 9-month-old, red silver smoke Maine coon — who resembles the wizard in both look and demeanor. “He’s majestic and powerful in appearance, yet incredibly affectionate, patient, and kind. He has a quiet confidence about him, almost as though he knows he’s something special,” said Robin Chatmas, owner of Aspen Maine Coons Cattery and Gandalf’s breeder. “And just like his namesake, he has a way of capturing everyone’s attention the moment he enters a room.” Robin Chatmas (right) and Jorge Garnica with Yellow Rose Cat Club show off Chatmas’ Maine coon, Gandalf the White, who won best cat in all breeds during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Gandalf the White sits on the judging table during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. This was Denver’s fifth-annual Cat Fest. About 6,000 cat lovers filled the National Western Complex on Nov. 15 to see rare breeds, visit the Mystical Egyptian Cat Temple, play cat bingo and connect with the local cat community. Gandalf won “Best Cat” among all the breeds in two competition rings. There were famous felines in attendance, too, like Baloo, who has 2.2 million Instagram followers. Fin the Adventure Cat, with 60,000 followers on the platform, made a spectacle for his fans, riding in a toy convertible car through aisles lined with hand-knitted kitten mittens, tiny cowboy hats, cat-themed T-shirts, mugs, keychains, socks and cat-ear headbands. Cat-themed booths fill the expo hall during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Colorado cat celebrity, Baloo, is fed by his owner, Cynthia Bennett, as he mingles with his fans during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Finn the Adventure Cat rides a toy convertible around Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. But the festival was about more than celebrities. To organizer Dana Cain, it was a place where cat lovers from walks of all nine lives could gather to celebrate their feline obsession, and possibly find a new companion. By 3 p.m., only a pawful of furry friends were left in the adoption booth cages, fulfilling what Cain said was the event’s “secret mission.” A total of 162 cats found a new home by the end of the six-hour-long festival; organizers have facilitated 842 adoptions in total since the event’s inception in 2022. “We have almost 20 adoption agencies and shelters there and we always give them free booths,” Cain said. Ashley Larson, practice manager at PetVet365, shows off her face paint while managing a booth during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Persian exotic shorthairs Gumball and Thomas hang out in on their table as they mingle with cat lovers during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Chatmas is not just a breeder developing perfect genetics. She is a self-proclaimed crazy cat lady who, for 50 years, has cared for strays, adopted feral cats and worked in shelters. This gathering gives her an opportunity to marry her newfound passion breeding Maine coons with her lifelong one — to find homes for as many cats as possible. “I’m all about adopting. Please go adopt from the shelters,” she said. “They all deserve a home.” A memory wall dedicated to pets who have passed away in the Mystical Egyptian Cat Temple during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Felipe Vieyra, employee at Yeepaw, holds Pumpkin Waffles, his newly adopted cat, wearing a Yeepaw cowboy hat during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Oriental shorthairs, June and Pluto, take a break from mingling with cat lovers during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Persian exotic shorthairs, (from left) Thomas, Gumball and Chili, hang out in on their table as they mingle with cat lovers during Cat Fest Colorado at the National Western Complex. Nov. 15, 2026. Editor’s note: This story has been updated the spelling of Robin Chatmas’ name.

title: Is Denver’s ponytailed Waymo avenger actually committing a crime?
summary: The DA’s office wasn’t so sure, but will have another look now.
content: An anti-Waymo vigilante appears to be at work in Denver — and the authorities aren’t sure they can prosecute him. The bearded, ponytailed avenger has a routine: He stops his Toyota Corolla in front of one of Waymo’s autonomous vans. Then, he hops out and grabs orange road cones from his trunk to trap the vehicle. Often, the unidentified middle-aged man wraps up by pelting the vehicle with eggs before driving away, leaving the robotic vehicle stranded. That’s all according to Det. Joseph Zahradnik’s investigation into complaints from the company. The Ojai model of the autonomous rideshare, Waymo, arrives at Alamo Placita Park in Denver on Aug. 19, 2026. An investigator for Waymo told Zahradnik that the company had “approximately 30 recorded incidents of the same suspect placing cones in front of Waymo vehicles and throwing eggs at the vehicles,” and was pursuing charges in seven of those cases, a police report stated. So far, the company hasn’t gotten its wish. Deputy District Attorney Philip Reinert found no criminal charges were appropriate, describing it as a civil matter. And when The Denver Post broke the story this week , a spokesperson for DA John Walsh put it this way: “Because there was no damage, we don’t believe that a crime was committed.” Meanwhile, Denver’s Luddite of the dairy aisle has won some fans online: “Some heroes wear ponytails,” one reader commented. So, does that mean everybody can throw eggs at Waymos? Not exactly. The “most obvious” charge would be criminal mischief, which requires “knowingly causing damage to the property of another person,” according to Jason Dunn, former U.S. Attorney for Colorado. The question is whether the company suffered damage or not. The yolk may not have ruined the clearcoat, but the Waymo representative told police the company had paid $800 to clean the vehicles — and perhaps as much as $2,000 — and temporarily removed the vehicles from service. “I think if it costs you money, it probably constitutes damage,” Dunn said. A Waymo taxi turns onto Sheridan Boulevard, from I-70. Aug. 16, 2026. But there’s also the question of prosecutorial discretion. Prosecutors simply may not have time or interest to pursue charges, Dunn said. “The DA’s office has to prioritize its prosecution efforts, and maybe a small incident like throwing eggs at a car is not where they want to put their resources,” Dunn said. “But on the other hand, when you have somebody who’s doing it, it sounds like dozens of times, then that probably should warrant a little more attention.” Colorado also has laws against blocking travel lanes, tampering with property and “throwing missiles at vehicles,” which includes anyone who “ knowingly projects any missile at or against any vehicle or equipment designed for the transportation of persons or property.” What happens next? The DA’s office initially told police that the matter was civil — telling Waymo’s investigator to take the unidentified man to court, basically. But a few hours after news of the egg-throwing broke on Tuesday, spokesperson Matt Jablow signaled Walsh’s office could change course. “We are collecting evidence regarding potential damage to the vehicles and will coordinate with the City Attorney’s Office to identify the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop,” he said. Denver police found the suspect’s vehicle was registered to a company that provides vehicles for lease by Lyft drivers, fueling speculation that the man works as a ride-share driver. A Waymo taxi turns onto Sheridan Boulevard, from I-70. Aug. 16, 2026. Robotic taxi fleets are growing quickly in cities around the U.S. and pose a significant risk to the livelihoods of human drivers. An initial study out of China found that traditional taxi drivers saw an 11% decrease in daily income after the introduction of robotaxi services. The impact in Denver isn’t clear yet. Waymo was operating only about 30 vehicles in Denver as of October, Denverite reported earlier. Autonomous vehicles also have become a symbol for some of a hegemonic tech state that has foisted artificial intelligence and constant surveillance onto the world. The vehicles can also be frustrating — sometimes blocking traffic and behaving unpredictably — or may simply be easy targets. On the West Coast, people have vandalized and torched Waymo vehicles, sometimes with people inside . Anti-autonomous activists also made a splash by incapacitating driverless cars with well-placed traffic cones .
